intro: To tailor a new grad nurse resume for ATS keywords, copy the skills and terms from one posting. Then match them only to work you have actually done. Recruiters often filter applicants with software, so the posting's wording counts. You do not need to buy anything. Word, Chrome, and an honest list of your clinical experience are enough.
tldr: Copy the skills, titles, and certifications from one posting into a table next to your master resume.
Use the posting's word only where it names work you really did.
Keep your real job titles. Never swap in a title you did not hold.
Check each keyword with ⌘F in Word, then export a PDF and copy its text to check the order.
Keep patient details out of resumes and AI tools. Follow your employer's rules on data.

blocks.text: What new grad nurse resume ATS keywords mean

An applicant tracking system, or ATS, is software that stores applications and sorts them for a recruiter. Keywords are the words in a posting that the software and the recruiter look for. Matching them means using the posting's own terms for work you really did, and nothing more.

You do not need a new resume for every job. You need one master file with every true detail, then a short copy for each posting. The copy uses the posting's skills, unit terms, and certifications where they fit your experience. That is the whole method.
Why your resume misses the posting

Most misses come from labels, not skill. Your program may say clinical rotation. The posting says med-surg experience and EHR documentation. You did similar work with different words. Many screening systems match words, not meaning, so the label matters.

Keep in mind where the figures come from. The Jobscan survey was run by a resume software company, so read its numbers as directional. It is the most specific public data on recruiter filters that I could check.
Build the master resume before you touch a posting

Open Word and go to File > New from Template. Search for Resume, then double-click a layout you like. Microsoft's support page describes this path for Word on Mac. Replace the placeholder text with every true detail you have.

items: Add each clinical rotation with the unit type, dates, and patient population in plain words.
List certifications with the exact name on the card, such as BLS or ACLS.
Add skills you can explain in an interview, such as medication administration or patient teaching.
Keep a second list of unit names, EHR systems, and shift types. You will need them for matching.
Do not cut anything yet. Cutting comes after you know which postings you want.

blocks.title: Keep patient details out
blocks.text: Keep patient details out of your resume and out of any AI tool. Describe cases by type, such as adult med-surg or post-op care, never by name or record number. Follow your employer's rules on data. If you are unsure, ask before you paste anything.
Pull the keywords from one posting

Pick one posting that fits. In Chrome, drag across the requirement text, then press ⌘C to copy it. Paste it into a Word file below your master resume. Delete the menus, ads, and benefit text, and keep the requirements.

Read it twice. The first pass finds skills. The second finds the nouns: unit names, EHR names, certifications, and shift types. Highlight each one. Terms that repeat across several postings are worth keeping in your master file.

rows: Clinical rotation on an adult med-surg unit
Experience bullet under your clinical heading
Charting in the EHR you used during clinicals
Skills section, plus the bullet that shows it
Skills section, only if you did them
Discharge teaching for patients and families
Experience bullet that names the result you saw
blocks.caption: Examples only. Replace each row with your own true experience.

blocks.text: Only match a term when you can explain it in an interview. If the posting says IV therapy and you started peripheral IVs under supervision, use that phrase. If you only watched a demo, say that instead.
Tailor the wording without making things up

Use the posting's word when it names the same task. Write wound management if the posting says that and you did wound care. Keep the rest of the sentence in your own words, so you can answer follow-up questions.

Keep your real job titles. If you held a nursing assistant or extern title, leave it as written. A short clarifying phrase after it can help. Never swap in a title you did not hold. Employers verify titles.
Check the file the way a parser reads it
A parser reads text in order, and layout can scramble that order. Columns, text boxes, and headers sometimes come out in the wrong place. A quick test shows you the problem before a recruiter does.

items: In Word, choose File > Export, pick PDF, and save the file.
Open the PDF in Preview. Press ⌘A, then ⌘C to copy all of its text.
Paste into Notes. Check that your skills and titles appear in the right places.
In Word, press ⌘F and search each term from your table. A miss means the term is absent or spelled differently.

blocks.text: Microsoft's release notes for Word for Mac list version 16.114.3, dated October 27, 2026, with quality fixes only. Check your version under Word > About Word if a menu looks different from these steps.
Mistakes that waste the effort

items: Stuffing a keyword list at the bottom. It reads as padding and hides your real experience.
Copying the whole posting, including boilerplate and benefits. Those lines do not describe your work.
Claiming a unit, device, or skill you never used.
Sending a file you never checked as a PDF. Columns and boxes may have dropped text.
Tailoring so hard the resume stops sounding like you. The interviewer hears the gap.

blocks.text: Residency applications need the same match

If a residency asks for a resume and a cover letter, run the same method on both. Use the posting's stated priorities in the cover letter, and keep each claim to something you did. A cover letter that repeats the resume word for word wastes the space.
When tailoring is not the real problem

If you match well and still hear nothing, look at the wider picture. The posting may have closed, or the unit may have filled. The research I could check does not publish applicant counts for nurse residency positions. You cannot tell how crowded any one posting is, so do not treat silence as a verdict on your resume.

Fit matters after the offer too. A systematic review of nurse residency programs reported first-year retention from 77.27% to 96.5% across studies. The studies were not randomized, so they show association, not proof.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and it answers out loud. Hold fn to dictate clean text at the cursor in any app. It points, explains, guides, drafts, and dictates. It does not click buttons, edit your files, or operate other apps for you.

For this task, explanation and pointing do the most work. Ask what a posting wants, or where a section lives in Word. Use dictation to get a bullet down in your own voice, then check every fact against your real record. Lazur only knows what is on screen or what you say.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. That does not replace your employer's rules, so keep patient details out of anything you ask.
What to do next

Pick one posting this week and build the master file first. Then run the table on that posting only. If you want the Mac side of this, [Word for Mac](/apps/word) and [Google Docs](/apps/google-docs) show how Lazur handles documents. When you are ready, the [download page](/download) starts a free trial with no credit card.

faq.question: Do I need every keyword from the posting on my resume?
faq.answer: No. Match the terms that are true for you and that you can explain. A posting often lists more than you hold. Leave the gaps as gaps, and say what you do have in your cover letter or interview.

faq.question: Does Word for Mac have a tool that finds keywords for me?
faq.answer: Not one that Microsoft supports. Microsoft says Resume Assistant was removed from Word in 2022 and no longer works. For a starting layout, use File > New from Template and search Resume. The matching is your own work.

faq.question: Can I change my job title to match the posting?
faq.answer: No. Keep the title you held. You can add a short clarifying phrase after it, such as the unit or shift type. Changing the title itself is a false statement, and employers verify titles.

faq.question: Does tailoring actually get more callbacks?
faq.answer: The research I could check does not prove it. Vendors make claims about callbacks, but I could not trace their methods. Tailoring is a reasonable habit, not a guarantee of a reply.

faq.question: Can I paste my resume into an AI tool to match keywords?
faq.answer: Only if your employer allows it and the tool's rules fit your situation. Remove names, identifiers, and any patient details first. When in doubt, ask your manager or privacy office before you paste anything.

faq.question: Should I send a PDF or a Word file?
faq.answer: Send what the posting asks for. If it accepts either, a PDF keeps the layout you chose. Test the PDF text before you send it, as the parser section shows.

faq.question: How long should a new grad resume be?
faq.answer: A single page is the usual target for a new grad. Each line should earn its place. If a line does not match this posting, it can wait in the master file.

faq.question: Can Lazur check my resume against a posting?
faq.answer: Lazur explains, points, and drafts when you ask. It does not click buttons or edit your files. You check each line against your real record yourself.

costs.title: A generic resume can miss the skills filter
costs.text: Jobscan's 2025 survey found that over 99.7% of recruiters use filters in an applicant tracking system or similar tool. Skills were the most common starting filter, at 76.4%. A resume that never uses the posting's skill words may never reach a person. You get no error message, only silence.

costs.title: A title mismatch can hide real experience
costs.text: Jobscan reports that 55.3% of recruiters use job titles as a filter. If your title does not match the posting's wording, a filter can skip you. The fix is a short clarifying phrase after your real title, not a new title.

costs.title: Tailoring takes time you may not have
costs.text: You work shifts, study for the NCLEX, and apply in batches. Matching a posting takes a focused sitting, and it competes with rest. Skipping it saves time now and can cost you interviews later.

costs.title: Overclaiming can cost you the offer
costs.text: A skill you cannot explain becomes a problem in the interview. Hiring managers ask follow-up questions about practice. A keyword you cannot defend does more harm than a missing one.

costs.title: A poor fit has a price for everyone
costs.text: A 2024 analysis of a South Korean cohort found 21% turnover among 586 nurses, with 123 leaving. That study is South Korean, so treat it as context, not a US rate. Still, a job that fits your skills and your unit is worth the extra care.

costs.title: Tired brains skip steps
costs.text: A Canadian study of new graduate nurses found cynicism rose from 1.55 to 1.79 on a 0 to 6 scale over one year. That is a measured change, not a verdict on you. When you are worn down, a long task gets dropped. A master file makes each later application shorter.

causes.title: Screening matches words, not meaning
causes.text: Many screening systems match the words in a posting against the words in your file. A phrase like good teamwork may not match interdisciplinary collaboration unless both appear. Recruiters read the file afterward, but the filter often decides who gets read first.

causes.title: Your school and the posting use different labels
causes.text: Programs say clinical rotation, capstone, or skills lab. Postings say med-surg experience, EHR documentation, or patient teaching. The work overlaps, but the labels do not. Matching depends on labels, so you have to translate your own experience.

causes.title: New-grad postings list more than one new grad holds
causes.text: Residency and new grad postings often stack requirements. A new grad may hold only some of them. That gap makes the whole posting feel closed to you. Match on the items you hold, and skip the rest without guilt.

causes.title: Old tutorials describe a Word feature that is gone
causes.text: Microsoft removed Resume Assistant from Word and announced it on August 9, 2022. Older guides still show steps to turn the pane on or off. Those steps no longer apply. Microsoft's current route to a starting layout is File > New from Template.

causes.title: Templates can scramble the reading order
causes.text: Some resume templates use columns, text boxes, or headers. A parser may read those in an order you did not intend. A plain layout is usually safer. You can test any layout by copying its text out, as the fixes section shows.

causes.title: Tiredness makes the match feel too big
causes.text: A Canadian study of new graduate nurses reported rising cynicism over one year. When you are worn down, tailoring looks like extra work. Then it gets skipped on the postings you care about most, which is the worst place to skip it.

fixes.title: Write one master resume first
fixes.text: Keep a long file with every true detail. Include rotations, units, skills, certifications, EHR names, and any unit projects or committees. For a starting layout, open Word and go to File > New from Template, search for Resume, and double-click one you like. Cut later, not now.

fixes.title: Copy each posting into a matching table
fixes.text: Open the posting in Chrome. Drag across the requirement text, press ⌘C, then paste it into a new Word file. Make a table with three columns: what the posting says, your true match, and where it goes. Fill it in for one posting at a time.

fixes.title: Use the posting's word for work you did
fixes.text: If you did wound care and the posting says wound management, use wound management. Keep the detail that shows what you did, such as the dressing type or the unit. The posting's word should describe your real work, not replace it.

fixes.title: Keep titles true and add context
fixes.text: Keep the title as it was. If a title is unclear to outsiders, add a short phrase after it, such as the unit or shift type. Never change the title itself to match the posting. Employers verify titles, and a mismatch can cause problems later.

fixes.title: Place keywords where they belong
fixes.text: Put matched terms in the skills section and in the experience bullets that show them. Do not hide words in white text, comments, or the footer. That reads as a trick, and it hides your real experience from the person who reads it.

fixes.title: Check every keyword with Find
fixes.text: In Word, go to Edit > Find > Find, or press ⌘F. Search each term from your table. A miss means the term is absent or spelled differently. In Google Docs, press ⌘F to run the same check in Chrome.

fixes.title: Test the file the way a parser reads it
fixes.text: Choose File > Export in Word and pick PDF. Open the PDF in Preview, press ⌘A, then ⌘C. Paste into Notes and read it top to bottom. If your skills or titles jump around or go missing, simplify the layout and test again.

fixes.title: Save one file per posting
fixes.text: Name each copy with your last name, the role, and the unit, such as Lastname_RN_MedSurg. Keep the master file separate. When you send the resume in Outlook, attach that exact file, so you always know what each employer received.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Build the master file
plan.text: Open Word and go to File > New from Template. Search for Resume and pick a plain layout. Fill in every true detail you have, including rotations, skills, and certifications. Do not cut anything yet.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Save a handful of postings
plan.text: In Chrome, open the postings you would actually take. Copy each requirement section into its own Word file. Note the unit, shift, and title exactly as the posting writes them.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Build the matching table
plan.text: Read the saved postings side by side. Highlight skills, certifications, unit names, and EHR names. Put terms that repeat across postings at the top of the table, then fill in your true match for each.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Tailor one resume
plan.text: Choose the best-fit posting. Copy the master file, rename it, and cut the lines that do not match. Apply the posting's wording only where it names work you did.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Check, export, and send
plan.text: Press ⌘F in Word for each keyword from the table. Export a PDF, copy its text, and read the result. Attach that PDF in Outlook, or upload it where the posting asks.

plan.label: Ongoing
plan.title: Update the master after each shift
plan.text: Add new skills and sign-offs to the master file as you get them. Each later application then starts from a longer list, and the copying gets faster.
